comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
# Browser-owned delegation: constraints on D2

A **harness** does the agent/model/tool work; an **environment** is where that harness runs and obtains its capabilities. **Many harnesses can run in one environment.** Putting Voicebox on a server to reach Paul's machine chooses one deployment. It must not make a server part of the shared harness contract. This note constrains the existing D2 ACP work, `voicebox-beads-6co`; it does not propose a second delegation implementation.

> “there is a world where there is zero server and it's all run locally on the client, and that has to be a hard requirement.”
>
> — Paul, relayed by coord, 2026-09-21, seq571

**Record:** `voicebox-beads-8fv.1`. **Status:** design and source inspection only; no browser delegation implementation or new runtime experiment. The quote is also in the bead. The current D2 clarification explicitly permits direct remote model APIs: *zero Voicebox server or local bridge* is the hard requirement, not necessarily offline inference. No further choice between a universal client or server architecture is pending. D9 conversation injection and D10 post-harness lifetime remain separate decisions.

Sources inspected: author D1 `c44c1de4118a93c382294cacf70b5d529b425004`, landed main `58a37358e514a0b5a140dcad8749861732371cef`, and D2/configuration bead descriptions captured on 2026-09-21. Earlier [delegation](delegate-task-plan.md) and [environment](environments-plan.md) plans remain history; Paul's dictated appendix was not changed.

## 1. What this changes in D2

D2 is **“Environment-owned async ACP client, ONE admitted adapter (stdio)”**. Its 08:52 UTC clarification already says that stdio is the first machine adapter, not the shared-library transport contract. That direction is correct. The remaining change is to make the separation executable rather than infer it from a Node-only success.

| D2 clause | Keep or change |
|---|---|
| Environment owns asynchronous work; admission returns a durable handle | Keep. An HTTP request, page view or ACP connection must not become the task's identity. The executing environment owns the record and runs the admitted harness instance. |
| ONE admitted real adapter, initially stdio | Keep as the first **machine binding**. Do not make spawning a process a prerequisite for constructing/importing the harness or admitting a browser-capable configuration. A browser selecting that stdio-only adapter refuses before dispatch. |
| ACP client learned from CAP, not imported wholesale | Keep. Separate ACP state/framing/validation from process, filesystem, socket and credential I/O. A local in-page tool call does not need an invented ACP subprocess. |
| Cancel during a turn settles cancelled | Keep the outcome requirement, but require observed turn settlement. Sending `session/cancel`, rejecting a promise or aborting a signal is not itself proof that effects stopped. Unknown effects remain interrupted/unknown; D6 owns the broader cancellation surface. |
| Surface: `lib/` + `server.mjs` | Expand to the shared loop/task contracts plus environment bindings. `server.mjs` becomes one caller of the shared lifecycle, not its only owner. Browser storage/auth/lifetime cannot be implemented by importing Node I/O. |
| Placement decision blocks transport design | Superseded. `voicebox-beads-3uq` now owns implementing the portable protocol decision, not asking Paul to choose one placement. |
| A real adapter completes one bounded task | Necessary machine acceptance, insufficient zero-server acceptance. Also require browser import and same-page lifecycle conformance with every Voicebox API/bridge unavailable. Label fixtures; they do not establish a real browser agent. |

D2 consumes `voicebox-beads-8fv.2`'s configured-agent record; it must not create another registry. Stable configured-agent IDs, harness implementation/version, model reference, executing environment and observed readiness belong there. D3 exposes that inventory. A configured agent is not its transient ACP session, and neither is an environment key.

**N18 is a source gap, despite `mzs` being closed.** At inspected main, `server.mjs`'s `/api/turn` still owns `resolveTurn → execute`; `public/fused.js` posts turns to that endpoint. `lib/resolver.mjs` exports resolution, not the whole lifecycle. The N18-labelled test checks that `core/` imports nothing outside itself. That proves a useful import boundary, not delivery of the importable loop described by `mzs`. D2/3uq need the actual entry point and a browser drive of it, not a closure citation.

## 2. Ownership and the shape of a call

Keep these identities separate:

- **Environment key:** the existing stable self-issued identity contract. The browser binding persists its own key; it must not use the shared string `local`, a tab title or an origin URL as identity.
- **Configured agent:** the stable configuration from 8fv.2. Renaming it must not retarget a task.
- **Harness instance and execution generation:** the live loop/session and its current incarnation. Several instances can share an environment. Killing one must not mark its neighbours dead.
- **Authenticated principal and authority epoch:** who may issue/read this task under current grants. Neither an environment address nor a harness ID proves that authority.
- **Task, root and attempt:** the immutable accepted work, the captured root binding, and the executing attempt. A new page connection changes none of them.

For the minimum tab-owned profile, several harness instances can run under one browser environment runtime. Its task service owns admission, aggregate capacity and storage serialization; each harness does not create an independent eight-slot allowance or an independent task database. A profile/origin may retain several named logical environments, but their identity/storage mapping needs an explicit rule. Do not accidentally assign every new tab the same singleton key, or mint a new environment for every observer connection.

### Envelope

Retain the existing call concepts: version, call ID, executing environment, admitted descriptor/configuration reference, tool, arguments and bounds echo. The receiver resolves those references against **its** current admission; the echo is not a grant. `delegate_task` model arguments remain bounded agent/task/context data. Owner, root authority, command, cwd, token, endpoint and execution generation are not model arguments.

The authenticated caller context accompanies delivery through the trusted transport/host binding, separately from model-controlled data. For a remote call it comes from verified pairing; for a local call it comes from an explicitly entitled caller/port created by the browser host. The receiving environment still checks authority on every status read. Do not permit the caller to manufacture that context by adding `owner` to an object.

There is a source ambiguity to settle in 3uq before extending the wire: `core/wire.ts` describes `CallEnvelope.environment` as **the environment asked to act**, while `lib/channel.mjs` describes stamping the channel's **own** environment. These agree for a co-located call but do not define a cross-environment caller/target split. Specify the executing target unambiguously and verify it against the receiving binding; retain authenticated source identity separately. If the published shape needs two identity fields, version it. The strict v1 parser must not silently start accepting extra authority fields.

An accepted response reports observations: address, executing environment, pinned root, queued state and confirmed record position. It is not permission for future effects. Status, progress and final results correlate to the same task/harness/attempt; a notification channel is replaceable. Opening another view must never resubmit the task.

### When both sides are in the same page

```text
harness A
  → trusted caller binding
  → the same admission/authority/bounds checks
  → environment task service → confirmed queued record → return handle
  → admitted harness B, scheduled independently
  → mediated tool effects and recorded observations
```

The transport can be an ordinary asynchronous function or a transferred `MessagePort`. No localhost socket, health endpoint, JSON-over-HTTP ceremony or server token is needed just because the contract is called a protocol. `createExecutorDoor` already accepts object input and normalises it; preserve its validation rather than introduce a permissive local shortcut. A direct invocation still needs an entitled caller context. WebMCP could expose the same admitted functions later; it is not required for the architecture and does not supply the permission boundary.

Keep expensive inference/Wasm execution off the interaction thread. A worker solves scheduling/isolation of execution from the UI; it does **not** by itself sandbox arbitrary same-origin agent JavaScript. Trusted loop code interpreting model output as data can use mediated tools. Admitting arbitrary generated JavaScript requires a separately demonstrated boundary. Wasm's restricted imports are useful only when the actual imports, wrapper and network paths are bounded.

## 3. Persistence without a machine filesystem

D1's ordering survives the move:

```text
validate caller, root, configuration and enforceable bounds
→ atomically exclude conflicting admission/retry
→ append and confirm the captured task record
→ settle the admission response
→ schedule execution
→ append observed transitions; never replay on read/reopen
```

The async storage operation changes the implementation: no result may escape while a transaction/write is still pending. Input, policy and configuration must be captured before awaiting persistence; later UI/configuration changes must not widen them. Dispatch and effects still recheck current authority within that captured ceiling; a snapshot does not defeat later revocation. Read-only views use the original root, never whichever project is currently selected. D4 context manifests remain separate; D1 currently refuses nonempty context rather than pretending references were captured.

**Keep one authoritative event history.** The smallest candidate is to adapt the existing OPFS/root audit for task events, with serialized writes, strict parsing and a defined confirmation operation. IndexedDB already holds picked-folder handles and can hold identity/credential references. Do not also persist a competing task-state table and then reconcile two sources of truth. If measurement favours IndexedDB transactions for the browser audit, move the authoritative browser event history there deliberately; projections/exports are not another authority.

Existing browser methods are not sufficient unchanged:

- `browser/storage.ts::readLines` catches every read error and returns `[]`.
- `browser/worker.ts::readAudit` drops entries that fail parsing.
- `appendLine` reads a length, writes using `createWritable({keepExistingData:true})`, then closes. It has no multi-context admission transaction or D1-style file/directory flush contract.

For tasks, missing history, unreadable history, torn history and permission loss must be different outcomes. As coord put it, **“an error read as an absence is a fail-open wearing a fail-closed name.”** A corrupt log cannot be treated as a fresh sequence or permission to start again.

Storage claims must name the platform guarantee. IndexedDB exposes strict/relaxed durability modes; strict requests confirmation to persistent storage, while relaxed can complete after handing changes to the OS. This is not a portable promise of immunity to power loss. OPFS needs its own measured close/flush contract, including contention and failure. `navigator.storage.persist()` concerns eviction, not process survival; denial, quota exhaustion, user-cleared storage and private-browsing loss remain possible. [S1–S2]

Root identity also needs a browser binding: keep `RootDescriptor`'s OPFS/handle kinds, preserve the owning environment, and retain the actual captured handle/root incarnation where needed. Recreating a directory under the same label/path must not silently adopt an older task. The machine's device/inode check has no fictitious browser equivalent; handle identity and delete/recreate behaviour need a targeted drive.

## 4. Credentials and access

The current server deployment keeps its pairing bearer in the host and proxies browser calls. That remains valid there. A zero-server deployment cannot require that proxy, a `.host-token` file, or a backend that mints every local call.

For local work, the trusted browser environment supplies a local owner/grant context and keeps its identity/sealing material outside model-visible tools and task records. Web Crypto plus IndexedDB is a candidate for persistent key custody. A non-extractable `CryptoKey` prevents raw export through the API; it does not prevent hostile same-origin code from using the key or forwarding a key object. The Web Crypto specification explicitly warns about script injection and cross-origin sharing through `postMessage`. An IDB database name or a separate same-origin worker is not a secret boundary. [S5]

Consequently, keep credentials and root handles out of agent contexts, inventory, audits, model prompts and public message payloads. Keep untrusted executable code away from the trusted origin's ambient storage/network authority. Browser grants must be checked when used, including after a reload. A picker handle persisted yesterday is not today's read/write permission. I3 still determines revocation semantics; neither the task seal nor cached configuration overrides current revocation.

For a remote model, choose a provider-supported browser credential flow and a bounded direct connection, or name the missing capability. An OAuth public-client flow or appropriately scoped browser credential may fit; a provider requiring a secret backend exchange does not fit the zero-server profile unchanged. Do not silently introduce a bridge as a fallback. On-device inference avoids a vendor credential but still depends on observed API/model/hardware availability. This note chooses neither a provider nor a credential-rotation protocol.

The task address remains a locator, not a bearer grant. A browser address should resolve through the owning environment's protected store/binding rather than require a machine path inside it. Preserve compatibility for existing D1 handles; changing their interpretation is a versioned migration, not a renderer change. Clearing the owner key/store cannot result in anonymous adoption. Another browser profile has neither the private origin storage nor the original authority: it must refuse unless an explicit transfer/pairing mechanism exists. D1's two-profile server-proxy test is not a serverless cross-profile guarantee.

## 5. What interrupted means when a tab closes

For an executing environment owned by a document/dedicated-worker lifetime, closing that document can end execution while the saved task remains. No close handler is required to run. On the next authorized opening, reconcile the prior nonterminal task to **interrupted, outcome unknown** only when the execution owner can no longer continue under its old generation. Never turn absence of a heartbeat into proof of death and never replay the prompt to discover what happened.

Several cases must remain distinguishable:

| Event | Required interpretation |
|---|---|
| Observer/message port closes; executing environment remains alive | Record stays addressable to another entitled connection; does not inherently cancel execution. D10 may later impose an explicit disconnect policy. |
| One harness stops while other harnesses share the environment | Reconcile only that harness's attempts. Environment-wide failure would be false. |
| Page is hidden, frozen, background-throttled or in bfcache | Not evidence of death. State may be old; report unconfirmed liveness rather than fabricate a terminal outcome. Recheck deadlines and authority before effects on resume. |
| Owning document/worker is destroyed and a later instance opens the store | Confirm/fence the old execution generation, then record interrupted without dispatch. If that confirmation is unavailable, return an honest owner-unconfirmed refusal. |
| The original runtime actually survives elsewhere | Query it under the recorded authority. Do not both resume it and start a replacement. |
| Origin storage/key is lost | Record/owner unavailable, not an empty successful task or an invitation to replay. |

A possible coordination mechanism is Web Locks for short storage critical sections and a separately held execution-ownership lock, plus a persisted generation checked at every mediated effect/transition. **Do not use a lock's availability alone as proof of process death.** Code may release locks before freezing; Chrome recommends doing so. `steal` explicitly permits prior code to continue without exclusivity, so it is not a safe death detector. A takeover must make stale generations unable to issue further mediated effects, and may still have unknown in-flight effects. Worker termination details and freeze/reacquisition races require browser experiments. [S3–S4]

Do not hold one exclusive lock for all harness computation: many harnesses may run in one environment. Serialize the records that actually conflict and bind execution ownership to the relevant runtime/harness/attempt. Aggregate environment budgets still apply.

A SharedWorker may change which page owns the work, but is not a promise of indefinite survival after the last client disappears. A service worker is event-driven and may be terminated while idle; calling it a durable worker does not make an arbitrary agent turn durable. No browser-only binding may promise compute continues after the browser is closed. [S6] D10 can choose among lifetimes the environment can actually provide; it cannot select an impossible one by metadata.

## 6. Specific moves, with existing homes

These are design findings attached to D2/3uq, not a separate markdown task tracker.

| Current file or concept | Required move | Existing work it constrains |
|---|---|---|
| `core/tasks.ts::TaskRecord.pid`, `boot`; `reduceTask` requires `root.kind === "machine"` and a `machine:` root string | Keep shared state/input/terminal rules; represent harness/attempt/generation independently of OS process metadata. Validate the captured root's portable identity, retaining per-writer sequence rules. | D2, D7, 3uq |
| `lib/tasks.mjs::createTaskHost`, Node fs/path/crypto, `process.kill`, `setImmediate` | Separate shared admission/run/reduction from confirmed event storage, authenticated caller context, executor and lifetime bindings. Node keeps realpath/device/inode/fsync/PID observation; the browser implements real platform equivalents or refuses. No fake PID, Node polyfill or second task engine. | D2, 3uq |
| `server.mjs::SELF_ENVIRONMENT`, `.host-token`, paired `/api/execute` | Keep the existing self-identity contract. Supply browser-owned identity/auth/sealing through its binding; do not expose the machine host token or confuse environment identity with owner proof. | I3, 3uq, 8fv.2 |
| `server.mjs` `/api/turn`, `execute`, live tool callback; `public/fused.js::turn` | Move the shared cycle into the actual importable harness library. HTTP/live/page entry points call it. Runtime I/O, UI rendering and provider selection stay outside that cycle. | D2 + N18 delivery verification |
| `lib/channel.mjs`, `core/wire.ts` | Define caller versus executing-target identity; preserve strict parsing and bounds validation for direct object, port and remote transport. Remove transport assumptions from shared ownership, not the authority checks. | 3uq, D2 |
| `browser/storage.ts::readLines`, `appendLine`; `browser/worker.ts::readAudit`, `appendAudit` | Add a confirmed, fail-closed task/audit path with explicit missing/corrupt/permission errors and writer coordination. Protect private task/credential namespaces against generic tool read/write. Do not use the current swallow/filter path as admission evidence. | D2 storage binding, D7 |
| `browser/idb.ts`, OPFS/picked-root registry and mutable `current` in `browser/worker.ts` | Persist environment/credential/root bindings without task-state duplication; task reads use captured roots. Define and drive same-path replacement, lost handles, grants and corruption. | 3uq, I3, D7 |
| Global executor registration and per-`createTaskHost` active map | Environment-owned shared admission/capacity, distinct harness instances and per-attempt lifecycle. Multiple harnesses must not multiply limits or reclaim each other's tasks. | D2, 8fv.2 |
| `core/environment.ts` browser/server kind, origin/reach and server-oriented refusal text | Reuse the descriptor. Browser kind already exists and need not have an origin endpoint. Represent in-process reach/lifetime and measured capabilities without treating every absence as a stopped HTTP service. | 3uq, configuration/discovery |
| `lib/commands.mjs`, live/text declarations and native task dispatch | Keep one admitted command path with correct caller context. Do not advertise a callable browser delegation tool before the browser binding can authenticate, persist and enforce it. | D2, D3, existing catalogue work |
| Browser delivery/type stripping and static resources | Produce a browser-importable artifact from the same source; no runtime Vite, Node TS transformer, `/api/turn` or hidden bridge dependency. Static asset delivery is not a running Voicebox task server. | N18 verification, 3uq |
| Existing D1 tests and `docs/10-delegate-task-d1.md` | Retain machine evidence; add portable conformance and browser lifecycle tests. Document machine-only guarantees rather than generalise fsync/PID or paired-proxy success to a tab. | D2 acceptance |

No generic transport framework or plugin container is required by this list. Start with explicit injected functions where the existing code touches platform facts. Keep `core/` free of platform imports and also test the shared runtime entry point; a clean `core/` cannot compensate for a server-only orchestrator.

## 7. Acceptance additions to record on D2

1. Import the same loop/task-lifecycle implementation in Node and a real browser with no Node globals or running Voicebox API/bridge. Static assets may be preloaded; every runtime backend attempt is observed and fails the test. A deterministic closed adapter establishes the lifecycle contract, **not** production model/ACP acceptance.
2. Run two configured harness instances in one environment. They have distinct instance IDs, share aggregate limits and current admission, and neither consumes the other's responses or terminal state. Drive one browser instance through the same contract.
3. Browser admission returns only after confirmed persistence, before held work finishes. Open an independently entitled port/view in the same storage partition; read the same task, close the first observer and read again. Another principal or profile with only the handle refuses.
4. Abort/quota-fail persistence, corrupt a record and simulate permission loss. Each refuses before dispatch; no empty-history reset. Concurrent duplicate call IDs produce one admission/dispatch, and changed content conflicts.
5. Actually destroy the owning tab/worker, reopen retained storage and observe interruption without replay. Separately freeze/resume and exercise bfcache: neither may be mislabelled death. Include a stale-generation late-effect attempt and another still-running harness as controls.
6. Block machine processes/stdio in the browser profile and select the machine-only configured agent: named refusal, zero hidden bridge requests. The separate machine run still drives the exact configured ACP adapter/version, bounded completion and observed cancellation.
7. Inspect disclosure: no provider/root credential in model context, event history, inventory or task address. Test an entitled local call positively; reject fabricated owner/config/bounds data. Exercise direct browser-provider custody only with a supported flow, without treating a fixture as vendor acceptance.

The first machine adapter may satisfy its scoped D2 implementation slice. It cannot close the zero-server requirement until a real browser-capable harness/configuration has been exercised. Record that remaining acceptance on the existing protocol/configuration work, not a second ACP project.

## 8. Questions that remain

**Policy/configuration decisions:** the stable browser environment's scope across tabs and storage partitions; which credential flow establishes its local/remote principal; which provider/agent is actually browser-capable; required browser/device support; how authority rotation affects old task handles; D9's delivery surface and D10's lifetime policy. The current clarification already answers that remote model APIs are allowed; this is not a question to send back to Paul again. A fully offline voice/model configuration is a stronger, separately measured capability.

**Cannot be settled by this document:** confirmation strength and latency of the chosen browser event store; interrupted-write and quota behaviour; picked-root replacement identity; multi-tab admission races; freeze/bfcache/worker ownership and fencing; prompt/request cancellation versus residual effects; actual browser provider auth/CORS/protocol support. These require the bounded positive/negative drives above. No real client-only agent, transport or containment result is claimed here.

## Platform references

Retrieved 2026-09-21. These constrain the proposal; they are not this lane's runtime evidence.

- **S1:** [IndexedDB transaction durability](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IDBTransaction/durability) and [IndexedDB specification](https://w3c.github.io/IndexedDB/#dom-idbtransaction-durability).
- **S2:** [Storage persistence](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/StorageManager/persist) and [Storage Standard](https://storage.spec.whatwg.org/#storage-pressure).
- **S3:** [Web Locks: termination and steal semantics](https://w3c.github.io/web-locks/). Lock ownership coordinates cooperative contexts; it is not authentication or proof all prior effects ended.
- **S4:** [Chrome Page Lifecycle](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/page-lifecycle-api): frozen tasks, unobservable discards, unreliable close callbacks, and releasing locks before freezing.
- **S5:** [Web Crypto security considerations](https://www.w3.org/TR/WebCryptoAPI/#security-developers): persistent CryptoKeys, injection risk and structured-clone sharing across origins.
- **S6:** [Service Worker lifetime](https://w3c.github.io/ServiceWorker/#service-worker-lifetime) and [HTML worker lifetimes](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html#the-worker's-lifetime).

Modern-web guidance was consulted. Its installed skill is outdated; retrieved on-device/WebMCP guidance was treated as capability-specific, not grounds to promise support on every browser or to add a mandatory fallback server. No skill update, product fix or browser prototype was performed.

title: The pre-push gate's npm test stage has a 60s cap the suite exceeds under load — refusal does not name the timeout
description:
FOUND BY: isocan-qwen, pushing voicebox-beads-mo9 from ~/worktrees/voicebox-docs-check (2026-09-21). The pre-push hook did not fire; it ran the equivalent checks by hand and reported that rather than letting the push look gated.

WHY IT MATTERS: the gate exists because a red tree reached main once (013feb4). Since it was built (voicebox-beads-99l) it has refused at least five pushes, every one for a real cause — a stray directory in shared scratch, a dead served front, a front serving a different tree, a folder rendered with a trailing slash in already-merged code, and a served front lagging behind main. EVERY ONE OF THOSE WAS A PUSH FROM A WORKTREE OR THE CANONICAL CHECKOUT. Hooks are per-clone configuration, so a fresh worktree has no hook installed at all.

CONDITION: git worktree add creates a new gitdir with its own hooks directory (or none), so core.hooksPath / .git/hooks are not shared. The gate script exists and is correct; the invocation path is missing.

SCOPE: worktrees are how this fleet does nearly all its work — land worktrees, per-lane worktrees, review checkouts. So the 'in this clone' caveat from 99l is not an edge case, it is the common case.

FIX DIRECTION (not prescribed): set core.hooksPath to the canonical hooks directory in every worktree, or have the worktree helper install the hook, or make the gate a required CI check rather than a local hook. The last is the only one that cannot be bypassed by forgetting.

ACCEPTANCE: push a deliberately-red commit from a fresh worktree and confirm it is refused.

EVIDENCE: isocan-qwen report seq 18, 2026-09-21T07:30; the mo9 branch push at 28b027e.

CORRECTION BY THE ORIGINAL FILER, driven rather than inferred (isocan-qwen, 2026-09-21).

RETRACTED: 'the pre-push hook does not fire from a fresh worktree' is FALSE. core.hooksPath=.githooks is repo-shared config; the tracked hook RAN on a real push from ~/worktrees/voicebox-docs-check with full output. The original claim came from a tail -3 that truncated the gate's output — an inference where a look was available, which is the same failure class as the pipeline trap already in the lane rules ('a pipeline can hide the exit code that mattered'). Mine this time.

THE REAL DEFECT, driven: the gate's npm test stage has a 60-second cap. The suite is ~200 tests with several 2-5s live ones and EXCEEDS 60s on this box under fleet load. The filer's test push was REFUSED on that timeout while its branch push minutes earlier PASSED. So the gate is LOAD-SENSITIVE: intermittent push refusals driven by box load, presented as gate failures, with a message that does not name the timeout.

TWO STAGES, BOTH MUTE ABOUT CAUSE: coord's earlier 'fetch failed' refusal was the ACCEPTANCE stage (shared front not answering at that moment); the filer's was the TEST stage (60s cap). Same gate, two stages, both refusing without naming which stage or why.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE GATE'S REPUTATION: the gate's refusals have been treated as proof it works, and at least one of them is now known to have been a timeout rather than a real defect. The refusals that named a cause (stray directory, dead front, front serving a different tree, trailing slash, front lagging main) remain real; the timeouts are not evidence of anything except load.

FIX DIRECTION (revised):
(a) MEASURE the test stage's budget under load and make the refusal NAME the timeout rather than reading as a failure;
(b) consider a fast-lane subset for pre-push with the full suite on a separate signal;
(c) the stage's output must reach the pusher even when the stage times out — a timeout that swallows its own output is the silent-failure class in the gate's own plumbing.

ACCEPTANCE: a deliberately-red commit from a fresh worktree is refused for the right reason AND the refusal names the stage and the cause; and a push under load that exceeds the budget refuses explicitly as a timeout rather than as a failure.

title: I1b — stamp the SELF-ISSUED environment key, not the shared "local" constant, and re-drive the two-host disagreement end to end
description:
FOUND BY the independent review of g7c (feat/i1-explicit-actor @ 7c800c8f4b71), driven on two live servers. SELF_ENVIRONMENT = "local" (server.mjs) is a CONSTANT EVERY SERVER SHARES, so POST /api/root re-stamps every declaration with it: one descriptor claiming environment 'env-laptop-key' was posted to two servers, A re-stamped it 'local', B re-stamped it 'local', and B then wrote to the root A had claimed (write ok, nothing refused). The stamp itself is correct — it refuses foreign ownership injection — but the consequence is that NO REAL PATH can produce a root whose owner differs from the acting environment, so the refusal 'not-reachable-from-this-environment' shipped library-only. The gap is not 'we have not driven it': the identity that would create the disagreement does not exist server-side yet.

WHAT: the server stamps the SELF-ISSUED key from core/environment.ts — the stable identity the environments work already mints (a key, not a label; the same discipline the descriptor follows) — at declare/handshake, instead of the shared constant. Then the owned-vs-acting mismatch is expressible in production, and the refusal can fire.

DONE: A declares a root; B is asked to act on it; B's refusal is not-reachable-from-this-environment naming A's key, and NOTHING lands on A's root.

ACCEPTANCE (drive, do not read): (1) the reviewer's two-server probe re-run with two servers holding DISTINCT self-issued keys — the same descriptor posted to each keeps a DISTINCT owner, neither re-stamped to a shared string; (2) B's act on A's root refuses by name, the why names A's key, the write does not happen and the file is absent on disk; (3) A's own act still succeeds (the fix must not refuse the owner); (4) the stale-constant case: a declaration that carries a foreign key is still REFUSED or re-stamped to the declaring host's own key, never accepted as a claim of another machine's identity; (5) root-seam (17), channel (12), reachability-actor (8) and the full suite pass, npm run gate green on the pushed tree.

SURFACE: server.mjs (SELF_ENVIRONMENT, POST /api/root, the handshake path, and resolveEnvironment('local') which is a ROUTING name and must not be conflated with the identity), core/environment.ts (where the key is minted/read), tests/reachability-actor.test.mjs (add the two-host case alongside the existing contrast).

EVIDENCE: the reviewer's two-server probe and its output (ask coord for the probe path/transcript); plus this bead. Related: g7c (the shipped vocabulary), epic 2gq.

RESIDUAL, named not papered over: the acceptance item 'B's act on A's root refuses by name AND leaves the file absent on disk' is NOT yet producible, because no path exists by which a host comes to hold a root another host owns (a peer's descriptor from the registry, adopted as the active root). That path is the next slice; the identity it needs now exists per host. Evidence for that claim: the probe re-run above (B re-stamps, so B acting on its own copy is correct, not a refusal).

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
REVIEW CONFIRMED + TWO SHAPE DECISIONS (ds-flash-1b, on feat/i1b-self-key @ 83dcf63800ba).

**THE FINDING THAT RESHAPES THIS BEAD** (reviewer's, kept verbatim because it is sharper than what I wrote): the registry ECHOES foreign-stamped homes verbatim — parseEnvironment keeps 'home' as-is and GET /api/environments serves it — so the raw material for the missing path is ALREADY ON THE WIRE. Every root-creation site stamps environment: SELF_ENVIRONMENT and the opfs/handle spread copies only path and id, so a forged environment in a declaration body does not survive (driven: a declaration stamped env_peerA came back carrying the adopter's own key). The reviewer drove the nearest thing to the path I named — a descriptor whose home carries a foreign stamp, adopted via POST /api/root — and B WROTE into A's directory with no refusal, stamped B. So: **the next slice is not 'build a path', it is 'STOP RE-STAMPING ON ADOPTION'** — smaller and sharper than either of us wrote here. My 'not producible' claim is confirmed by exhaustive path-walk and drive, not by inference.

**DECISION 1 — the local row in /api/environments serves the MINTED KEY, and 'local' becomes a route rather than a second name.** Two identifiers for one host, visible side by side, is the drift shape of this whole week: a display value that looks like an identity, and the next reader picks the wrong one. So the row's 'key' is the identity (env_+16hex), and 'the host on this machine' is expressed by the flag that already exists (local: true), never by a second key. resolveEnvironment('local') stays accepted as a ROUTING input ('call the host on this machine') — routing by a name is fine; SERVING two names for one identity is not.

**DECISION 2 — /api/call by the minted key refusing 'unknown-environment' is an ARTEFACT of the implicit row, not the intended shape.** The local host is a host like any other and must be addressable by its identity. Intended shape: one host, addressed two ways (its minted key, or the routing name 'local'), ONE identity; the implicit row currently makes the identity unroutable while the alias works, which is backwards.

**Both decisions are 'decide and record', not bug fixes** — the reviewer states they are consistent with what is documented. The code for them is a small, named follow-up, not part of this bead's landed commit: (a) resolveEnvironment accepts SELF_ENVIRONMENT alongside 'local' and returns the local descriptor carrying the minted key; (b) the local row served by /api/environments carries key = SELF_ENVIRONMENT with local: true. Add them to the adoption change above as ONE next slice: 'stop re-stamping on adoption, and let the local host be addressed by its own key'.

**REVIEWER'S VERIFICATIONS RECORDED** (all in my favour, driven): 0600; env_+16hex; STABLE ACROSS RESTART; malformed content re-minted rather than falling back to a shared string — 'the fallback that would undo the fix does not exist'; and the harshest case for the key file, with the host directory declared as the active root, both a direct file read and a turn read refuse dotfile-refused.

title: DECISION (Paul): who presses the approval hand for extensions — the page can disclose but cannot hold the host token
description:
Found building the extension surface (voicebox-beads-vwb, feat/extension-surface): the page can DISCOVER (catalogue with plain verdicts), STAGE (sideload through the same admission gate), and DISCLOSE (the full plan: what it asks for, what it would get, what it cannot have) — but it can never APPROVE, because approval requires the host token (voicebox-beads-m2i) and the page must not hold it; that gate is what stopped the page admitting its own code in two fetches. So today the honest page shows the plan and says: the decision is made on the machine that runs the server. THAT IS A GAP A PERSON WILL FEEL: the surface shows 'waiting for review' and the person must walk to a shell to press the button.

THE DECISION: what is the approval surface? Options on the table: (a) the host pushes a confirmation to the page (the confirm-gate pattern — but then a compromised page could press yes itself, unless the confirmation carries something the page cannot forge); (b) a one-time approval token the person copies from the host into the page (the page presents the plan, the person pastes an approve-code); (c) the shell stays the approval surface and the page says so plainly (current state — honest but walks the person to a terminal); (d) the host TUI/daemon prompts on its own console. Whatever is chosen must keep the m2i property: the page alone cannot complete an admission, and the audit trail must name who actually decided.

WHAT EXISTS: the wasm-tools pipeline builds every tool from in-repo source, self-tests each
binary before shipping, and emits an installable module with a manifest (id/digest/bytes/
capability/description). install-shelf.mjs puts it on ~/.isocan/modules/wasm-tools, and
`isocan module ls` shows it LOADED with digests. hash and diff are on the shelf with real
digests, each verified by self-test and by an independent cross-check (zlib for compress).

WHAT IS MISSING: the tools are on a shelf and NOT in the agent's command catalogue. The
catalogue is what the menu, the CLI and the voice brief read; the shelf is a directory of
modules. Nothing bridges them, so a person can see the tools and the agent cannot call them.

THE FIX SHAPE: module tools should APPEAR IN the one command list, generated from the
manifest, with their capability and their limits, so the same list that feeds the menu, the
CLI and the voice brief also exposes the modules. That is the "one source of truth for what
can be done" rule applied to the tools that already exist.

DONE MEANS: a module tool is invocable from the voice/text path, its result is an addressable
item, and a refusal (unavailable module, digest mismatch, over-capability) is NAMED.

Built, driven, pushed: branch e1m0/one-root @ ef2396d (off main@4a74bdd, NOT stacked — the shared-log and E1-M0 work had landed by then). 47 checks green (npm run test:e1m0, +9); the repo's existing 11 unchanged.

THE SEAM, NAMED (core/root.ts): RootDescriptor = opfs | handle | machine, with ROOT_FACTS per kind as data — where the files are, who can SEE them, WHICH PEERS CAN ACT, the containment mechanism, whether a gesture is needed. resolveInRoot delegates to core/paths.ts (one containment implementation, '..' refused at any depth); the machine kind adds the realpath pass the design always said it would. reachableFrom refuses 'root-not-reachable-from-here' and NAMES who can act.

LOOP: the active root is state (GET/POST /api/root); write/read/list//api/file/api/files//api/audit all follow it; nothing writes to a folder nobody declared; and the loop keeps its own file in that root's .audit/ (one file per (root, writer)) — including its REFUSALS, because a log of successes cannot answer 'what did it try'.

PAGE: declares its root on open and adopt (whichever kind), so the loop learns it — and learns by name when it cannot act there; the header states the root kind and who acts on it; the explorer's machine panel follows the active root and refuses by name for a page-owned root.

DRIVEN: tests/root-seam.test.mjs (7) — default machine root; a loop write lands there AND is logged with observed bytes from the world; declaring another root MOVES the loop and the old root gains nothing; '..' at any depth AND a symlink out both refused (two passes); opfs/handle roots report reachableFromThisProcess false with write+listing refusing by name (why names the page); bad declarations named (path-missing / not-a-directory / unknown-root-kind / bad-request) and the active root unchanged. tests/one-root.test.mjs (2, browser) — the page declares a machine root THROUGH ITS OWN FORM, the loop writes there, the page shows it and refuses its own act by name; a picked folder declared the same way → the loop refuses by name, the page writes into the folder, containment still refuses.

HONEST LIMIT: the page cannot write into a real picked folder headlessly (prompt + no click can be scripted), so that half is driven through a handle root with implicit permission — same kind, same path, same refusal; the real folder is driven for declaration, reading, listing, refusal, containment. Nothing branches on test vs real.

AND: an independent vision check found a genuine UNTRUTH in the header — an OPFS durability line ('held until the browser decides otherwise') shown for a machine root. Fixed, plus a label collision and a subtitle that omitted the third kind; re-checked clean. No DOM assertion could have found it: the DOM contained exactly what the string said; the CLAIM was wrong.

RECEIPT: docs/evidence/one-root-20260920/RECEIPT.md. State: IN_REVIEW — needs a different lane.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
F-HYGIENE AND THE RETIRED DEFAULT — fixed at e1m0/one-root @ 3731589 (pushed). PROOF: npm test → 128/128 green; then git status --porcelain → EMPTY.

1. THE HYGIENE BLOCKER, fixed at the source rather than at the fixture. Cause was a real bug: the loop's log path is path.join(root.path, '.audit', ...) — right for a machine root, a VIRTUAL string for opfs/handle roots — so a refusal for an unreachable root wrote an entry into the process's cwd (the repo). Now the loop logs only for a root it can name (kind machine + absolute path); when it cannot, the entry is NOT written and that absence is reported (logged: null, logRefused), because a missing entry must be visible rather than silent. tests/root-seam.test.mjs runs the server in a scratch cwd and asserts it stays EMPTY after an unreachable-root refusal and after an undeclared act — pinned by the suite, not by a manual git status. The two committed artefacts are git rm'd, and v1/ is deliberately NOT gitignored: a future repo-relative write must show up loudly.

2. THE DEFAULT IS RETIRED. There is no fallback root: with none declared, every act refuses with 'root-not-declared' — a named sibling of root-not-reachable-from-here, kept separate because 'there is no root yet' is answered by the environment declaring one and 'that root is not mine' by the other side acting. VOICEBOX_WORKSPACE survives as an operator's DECLARATION at boot, not a default. The three files that leaned on the old default now declare their roots (two always did via a scratch dir; voicebox.test.mjs moved off the repo's workspace/ onto a scratch root it creates and declares, and extensions.test.mjs now creates the root it declares — a declaration names an existing folder, so a typo is path-missing rather than a new directory nobody asked for).

3. TWO MORE THINGS THE FULL GATE CAUGHT that my own suite could not: a generated doc block still quoted /api/health's retired 'workspace' field (the block now describes the SHAPE of the declaration — declared + root: {kind, path} — never a path, since an absolute path in a committed document is the defect that comment warns about), and my bare-server check collided with another suite's port (8842) — suites must not share a port, which isolated runs cannot reveal.

128 checks (the root-seam suite went 7 → 9). Receipt §6 records the finding, the cause, and the property.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
REVIEW COMPLETE (glm-flash-1, gate holder, read-only — no code changed). Scope: lib/live-session.mjs (383l), lib/live-providers/{gemini 148l, openai 195l, stub 76l}, plus the seam's call sites in server.mjs (1740-1830). Current main at review time: fdd3e58.

COMPOSITION VERDICT: the three fixes (rate declaration, null-proto registry + named unknown-provider refusal, running-session flag) COMPOSE with the g1l tool contract. Traced orderings all hold: rate refusal at first frame (server.mjs:1745-1750, named, close 1011) → readiness gate enforced BOTH sides (sendAudio + transport.send audio) → tool-call events gated on ready (an act that cannot be answered must not start) → sendToolResponse gated, with the host's loud log when acts landed but the answer could not be sent → terminate-once via hoisted function → late-ready refused → running-session flag cleared per-peer (the "first to leave reports the second as gone" fix). No gap found between the fixes. The factory-throw path (unknown provider, missing key) is also handled: named error to the page + close 1011.

FINDING 1 (real, composition gap): openai.mjs sendText (lines ~168-173) sends conversation.item.create + response.create UNCONDITIONALLY. The g1l-era tool path carefully defers response.create while a response is active or tool outputs are pending (responseActive/responsePending/resumeResponse — "OpenAI permits only one active response in the default conversation"), but sendText bypasses that scheduler entirely. Text typed mid-response or mid-tool-answer produces a competing response.create → vendor error → the user's text is dropped behind an error event. Gemini is unaffected (clientContent is queue-safe server-side). Fix belongs to the seam owner: route sendText's response.create through the same resumeResponse scheduler.

FINDING 2 (vendor-behaviour question — NOT settleable read-only): openai.mjs interrupt() sends response.cancel unconditionally, including when tool results are pending (executor still running). Whether the vendor then emits response.done (→ resumeResponse replays the pending outputs) or stays silent (→ the function_call_outputs are stranded until the next sendText) decides whether a barge-in during tool execution strands the answers. Needs one bounded live drive; I ran none (no vendor quota consumed).

FINDING 3 (minor): interrupt() with no active response sends response.cancel anyway → vendor error event surfaces as session error noise. Same fix site.

FINDING 4 (minor, two parallel registries): providers and REQUIRED_INPUT_RATES are separate maps — registration does not require a rate declaration; the failure moves to page-connect time. It IS loud there (named refusal + close 1011, server.mjs:1745-1750), and the stub provider hits exactly this if a page selects it — acceptable, but one registry or a registration-time assertion would remove the second failure site.

FINDING 5 (minor): resolvedLiveProviderName honours legacy LIVE_PROVIDER alongside VOICEBOX_LIVE_PROVIDER — if both are set to different providers, the newer wins silently. Documented in the comment; a startup log when the legacy name is the one chosen would surface it.

ENVIRONMENT-VS-SELECTION (coord's question 2): answered for the whole seam. The keys are read from process.env INSIDE the factories (openai.mjs:64, gemini.mjs:31): selection alone does not determine function — a selected provider whose key is absent throws at create. That throw IS handled: server.mjs catches it, names it to the page (type error + close 1011 "live session failed to start"). So the environment decides viability, and the page is told, by name. No other env-dependent branches found in the seam files (grep: OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, VOICEBOX_LIVE_PROVIDER, LIVE_PROVIDER only).

NOT EXAMINED: lib/ws-server.mjs internals (frame fragmentation/1003 — adjacent, outside the seam files); page-side audio-client.js; a live vendor drive (no vendor quota consumed — zero live calls run); test-suite coverage quality (I read the seam, not the tests' assertions); extension-admission interaction with live tools beyond the onToolCall executor hop.

title: The LIVE SESSION must be pluggable — Gemini Live today, OpenAI Realtime next
description:
PAUL, 2026-09-19: 'remember we also want to use gemini live, but it should be pluggable so we can also use open AI.'

CURRENT STATE: the live path is hard-wired to Gemini. lib/live-session.mjs exports LIVE_MODEL = 'models/gemini-3.8-live' and speaks the BidiGenerateContent protocol directly (setup with responseModalities AUDIO plus thinkingConfig, then realtimeInput audio frames both ways). There is no provider seam on this path — unlike the TURN path, which has one by design (lib/resolver.mjs registerResolver(name, fn), with provider 'script' today and a model resolver in flight).

SO THE ASK IS: give the LIVE path the same shape the TURN path already has. A provider seam where a live session is created behind an interface, with Gemini Live as the first implementation and OpenAI Realtime as a second. The contracts differ in detail (Gemini: setup + setupComplete + realtimeInput; OpenAI Realtime: session.update + conversation.item.create, different audio encodings and event names) so the seam has to be at the level of 'a live audio session' rather than 'a websocket that takes these frames' — otherwise the second provider is a rewrite, not a provider.

WHAT THE SEAM MUST PRESERVE, all of which are already proven properties of the current implementation and must not be lost by abstraction: (1) the READINESS GATE — audio before setupComplete is held and counted, never forwarded and never silently dropped (the 192-of-208 lesson); (2) the malformed-frame rule — one bad frame costs a frame, not the conversation; (3) the truthful state machine — disconnected must never read as listening; (4) the sticky refusal; (5) no hand-rolled resampler (the browser's own pipeline at 16 kHz in, 24 kHz out).

VERIFY BY DRIVING: the same page with the provider switched by configuration, both providers producing real audio, and the readiness gate holding on BOTH — a gate that only exists in one implementation is the drift this seam is meant to prevent.

RELATED: the protocol/placement decision (where the harness RUNS — also filed), N18 (the loop library, which is the same abstraction instinct on the turn path), and the thinking requirement (gemini-3.8-live accepts thinkingConfig; thinking is ON by default at ~50 thoughts tokens).

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
**Design note written: `~/journal/reports/voicebox-live-session-seam.md`** (147 lines) — the written seam, before code, as voicebox-ui flagged it needed. Not an implementation; no code changed.

**Reviewed at `615b301`** (branch `docs/reflect-system`), and **every claim about the current implementation quotes file:line — 15 references, all verified by reading the line back** (`lib/live-session.mjs:25,29,46,48,49,66,68,92,99`; `lib/ws-server.mjs:55,84`; `lib/resolver.mjs:14`; `public/audio-client.js:19,20`; `public/pcm-worklet.js:2`).

**The four things the brief asked for:**

1. **The seam is a live audio session, not a socket that takes frames.** `registerLiveProvider(name, createSession)` mirrors the turn path's `registerResolver` (`lib/resolver.mjs:14`); a provider supplies `start/sendAudio/interrupt/close` and raises a **fixed event set**, of which only one is terminal — so a provider cannot invent a state the host does not understand.
2. **The five properties, with an owner each**: the **readiness gate** is **host-side** (`live-session.mjs:29,68,99` — counted, held, logged at gate-open), and so is the **malformed-frame rule** (`:66`, with the *different* fragment rule beside it at `ws-server.mjs:55`); the **truthful state machine** (`:92`) and the **sticky refusal** (`ws-server.mjs:84`) are host + provider duties; **no hand-rolled resampler** is a client property the seam must not break (`audio-client.js:19-20`). A gate implemented per provider is the drift this seam exists to prevent.
3. **What is genuinely different** — Gemini's setup/`setupComplete`/`realtimeInput`; **only `["AUDIO"]` is supported** for response modalities (`:46`), so no thought text reaches the client (`:56`); **thinking is on by default at ≈50 thoughts tokens** (`:48-49`) with no OpenAI equivalent → an **optional capability**, not an assumption. **OpenAI's audio rates are not verified here** — the note says so rather than assuming they match, and makes `rate` a provider-declared value, which is the first thing a second provider must state.
4. **The smallest falsifier, needing no OpenAI key**: a **stub provider** that delays `setupComplete`, sends one malformed frame, and closes with a code — then the **same page, one env var**, must reach ready, hold the gate, survive the frame, and show *disconnected* rather than *listening*. If the gate holds against a stub, the gate is demonstrably host-side; if it does not, the seam is at the wrong level and the note is wrong.

Three states are used throughout, as in the iiq finding: **exists today** / **designed, not built** / **neither**.

title: Settings surface: the cog back, plus mic-input and speaker-output pickers
description:
PAUL, 2026-09-19: 'in a previous version I saw a settings cog' and 'we also need the mic input and speaker output picker like in voice-agent in isocan.'

CURRENT STATE, measured: the page has ZERO settings surface — 0 mentions of settings/cog/gear in index.html and no enumerateDevices or deviceId anywhere in public/. The cog existed in an earlier design (astra's artefact carried a gear icon) and the rebuild dropped it, which is why Paul noticed its absence rather than its presence.

THE TWO HALVES:
1. THE COG — a settings affordance. The rebuild removed chrome deliberately (it was fixing 'no card borders, no panes' and the gear went with the furniture), so this is a case where one removal was right and another was collateral. It needs a considered home rather than being re-added to the top right because it used to be there.
2. DEVICE PICKERS — microphone input and speaker output, like isocan's voice agent. The reference implementation is ~/isocan/packages/voice-agent/src/main.ts and it contains a hard-won detail worth copying rather than rediscovering: it stores BOTH the device ID and the device NAME (isocan.voice.deviceId / deviceName, outputId / outputName), and its own comment says why — 'the id is what getUserMedia and setSinkId take; the name is what the page can still say about it afterwards. Headphones that leave take their id out of enumerateDevices() with them, and "<name> is not connected" is only sayable if the name was kept — which is the whole difference between a visible state and a silent revert to the system default.'

WHAT THAT MEANS IN PRACTICE, and it is the acceptance: unplug the chosen microphone and the page must SAY that device is gone by name, rather than silently falling back to the system default and looking like it is working. Same for the output. isocan also refuses to touch the DOM when a device poll changes nothing (a devicesSignature), and keeps an outputProblem string for 'a route the browser refused, said out loud rather than swallowed'.

ALSO RELEVANT: setSinkId on the output path is the difference between 'the model replied' and 'you heard it', so the picker is functional rather than cosmetic — and the mic choice interacts with the live session's 16 kHz AudioContext.

RELATED: the waveform meters landed 2026-09-19 (input wave + output ring) — the pickers sit naturally beside them, and both are about the same question: is the person's real audio hardware actually in the loop.

title: A better file explorer — and it must show WHICH root it is showing (OPFS, a picked directory, or the machine's filesystem)
description:
PAUL, 2026-09-19 (voice note): 'Thing to put in the beads as well for the voice box project is we need a better file explorer. We're going to get lots of files and projects that kind of come through. We're going to want to have either the OPFS or the directory handle or the native server system view as well.'

WHY NOW RATHER THAN LATER: the workspace is currently a flat directory listing in a pane (README: 'the workspace is a flat directory — no project scaffolding, no shell'), which was adequate when the loop could only create/read/list. Three things are landing that break it: N20 (a project root may be a PICKED DIRECTORY, not just OPFS), E1-M0 (projects with a layout, not loose files), and the agent loop becoming real (many more files arriving, from voice turns and from tools).

THE THREE VIEWS PAUL NAMED, and the reason they cannot be presented as one thing:
- **OPFS** — the page's origin-private storage. Access is implicit; no permission prompt; invisible to any other app.
- **A picked directory handle** — the user's REAL filesystem, chosen once via showDirectoryPicker(), persisted in IndexedDB so a reload does not re-ask, and possibly needing a fresh gesture to re-acquire. Different permission story, different failure modes.
- **The native server view** — the machine's filesystem as the zero-dependency server sees it. A third authority, and the only one that survives the page being closed.
A single listing that silently mixes them would be the 'weaker guard is more dangerous than its absence' shape: a person cannot tell what they are looking at, so they cannot reason about who can see it, what happens on reload, or what persists.

ACCEPTANCE, to be driven rather than described:
1. The explorer always states WHICH ROOT it is showing — the same requirement N20 imposes on the record, arriving from the UI side.
2. Switching roots is a deliberate act with the permission consequence visible (OPFS: none; picked: a gesture and a grant; server: the host's authority).
3. A file created by a voice turn is visible in the explorer immediately, and shows which root it landed in.
4. The three failure modes are distinguishable and named: permission denied, handle gone or re-acquire needed, root unreachable — never a generic error (the isocan-iiq lesson: three classes reaching the user as 'internal error').
5. Lots of files stay usable — pagination or search rather than an unbounded list, and it must not fetch the whole tree on every page load (the phantom-turn lesson: the page used 'read <name>' turns to build its own listing, which is how turns nobody typed ended up in the server's log).

RELATED: N20 (persistent directory handles — this is its UI half), voicebox-beads-6dw (E1-M0: project layout), the N18 loop library (files arrive from turns and tools), and docs/02-environment.md's environment table.

title: Portable harness protocol: implement Paul’s zero-server placement decision
description:
CURRENT DECISION (Paul, 2026-09-21): placement is answered. The harness must also run entirely in the browser with zero Voicebox server/bridge; the current machine-access deployment may remain server-side. This bead stays OPEN for its existing protocol specification and absent-side acceptance, not for another choice of placement. Browser direct-provider credential custody and lifecycle mechanisms must be specified, not bypassed. Browser-delegation detail is 8fv.1. Historical question below is preserved, not the current decision.

PAUL, 2026-09-19: 'I've still no clue how you're planning to do this kind of environment between the systems. I've seen the environment. Is there a shared protocol that is documented somewhere? I don't see it right now.'

THE HONEST ANSWER: there is no protocol document, and the reason is that it is deliberately UNDECIDED rather than forgotten. docs/06-dynamic-tools.md §3 is titled 'Where tools RUN when part of the agent is somewhere else — OPEN, deliberately', states 'This is not resolved and should not be read as a recommendation', and lays out four placements. docs/02-environment.md:186 adds the transport fact that constrains them: the browser environment has 'no harness' — a dedicated worker in the page, same tier table and audit code, wasm and JS tools, file reads/writes, generated assets; no processes.

SO THE PROTOCOL IS A CONSEQUENCE OF A DECISION NOBODY HAS MADE. Paul is asking for it, which means he wants the decision made and written down.

WHAT I WANT, in this order: (1) an OPTIONS PAPER — the four placements from §3 with what each buys, what it costs, and what it makes impossible later, plus the smallest running evidence that exists for any of them (the doc says there is one piece); (2) HIS DECISION; (3) then the protocol spec that falls out of it — the message shapes, the transport, the authority boundary between a page and a machine, and what happens when one side is absent, because 'the page is closed' and 'the server is down' must not be the same experience.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS: the loop library (N18) is shared across placements, and its whole point is that the same code runs in a machine process and a page worker. Writing the library before deciding where it runs risks building the wrong seams — and writing the protocol before the decision risks encoding the wrong authority model.

RELATED: N18 (the loop library), N15 (harness delegates to harnesses), N11 (environments; the browser is the first), docs/06 §3, docs/02 §1.7.
notes:
BINDING REQUIREMENT (Paul, 2026-09-21): the harness must run anywhere, including entirely in a browser client with zero Voicebox server or local bridge. Server deployment is allowed for machine access, not required by the shared contract. Placement changes available capabilities, transport, storage and lifetime; it must not fork the coordination semantics. A browser cannot spawn a stdio CLI; refuse that unavailable capability rather than hiding a server dependency. Zero server does not mean zero remote model API.
Paul answered placement on 2026-09-21: server is acceptable for current machine access; browser-only is a hard requirement. No further placement choice is pending. Keep this bead open for its existing protocol-spec deliverable: shared messages/authority, browser-direct credential custody, absent-server/tab lifetime cases and runnable client-only acceptance. Reconcile docs/02 section 1.1b and docs/03 section 3.4 (browser cannot spawn pi is true; browser cannot host any harness is false). N18/mzs is closed, but its browser-capable library delivery must be verified against main rather than inferred from closure. D9/D10 remain distinct undecided policies.

title: N20 — Persistent DIRECTORY HANDLES as the environment's root, not only OPFS
description:
PAUL, 2026-09-19: 'I know it says OPFS but we also need access to local file system using directory handles. It needs to be a clear task for the system to get through and build.'

THE REQUIREMENT IS IN THE BRIEF (docs/00-brief.md:348-381, N20, added 2026-09-20 06:00) WITH ITS OWN TABLE: OPFS vs a picked directory handle. Access to OPFS is implicit to the origin; a picked directory is granted once by the user through showDirectoryPicker(); the handle must be PERSISTED in IndexedDB, not held in a variable, so a reload does not re-ask; re-acquisition may require a click because a picked directory can need a gesture while OPFS does not. The brief's line that matters: 'A directory handle makes the machine's filesystem reachable to the tool that is supposed to build real things.'

WHAT IS MISSING IS THAT IT IS NOT A TASK. It is a paragraph in a brief and a row in a table in docs/02:186, with no bead, no owner and no acceptance — which is why Paul 'still sees no clear task for the system to get through'. This bead is that task.

ACCEPTANCE, to be driven rather than described: (1) a project whose root is a picked directory; (2) the handle persisted across a reload with no re-pick and no gesture; (3) containment enforced for the picked root exactly as for OPFS (the resolver refuses, never tidies — core/paths.ts now refuses any '..' segment at any depth, and that must hold for both root kinds); (4) the SAME project record can express both kinds — if the record cannot say which kind of root it has, the UI cannot report an honest recovery story, which is the failure N20 names; (5) the gesture/permission failure path reports why rather than failing generically.

RELATED: isocan's N20 (the same shape arrived there first), voicebox-beads-6dw (E1-M0, which owns the environment), and the containment work landed 2026-09-19.

title: N18 — Extract the agent loop into an importable library (client, server, and other placements)
description:
PAUL, 2026-09-19 (voice note): 'I did ask for a shared library that is essentially what the pi harness is. That is the agent loop, because we're going to use it across client and server. I don't see where any of this is right now. It just looks like it's all blurted out into live-voice or somewhere… the agent loop is going to be a really critical component and it's going to be shared across all the different environments, so it definitely needs to be abstracted out… that's the bit where there's extensions and we will integrate the extensions. And remember we said we're going to be able to build extensions just by using voice.'

BRIEF N18 VERBATIM: 'Make sure that the agent loop and the harness that we have is abstracted into a library in the project that can be imported and reused across client, server, and a bunch of other places as well. I think we're going to want consistency at that level. It's going to be an important part of the project.'

WHY IT IS A GAP, measured 2026-09-19 rather than assumed: there is NO loop module. core/ holds the ENVIRONMENT core (audit, paths, policy, project, tier-table) and is on the right path per docs/02 §1.7 ('pure data and small functions with a narrow dependency surface, because the same code has to run in a machine process and a page worker'). But the LOOP — turn → decide → dispatch → result → record — is spread across three places: lib/resolver.mjs (verb mapping), server.mjs (the /api/turn route and the executor call), and public/fused.js (page orchestration of the same cycle). Three copies of one cycle, in three languages of thought, is exactly the drift the brief warns about ('a core that runs in one placement becomes two implementations that drift').

DELIVERABLE: an importable loop library — one module, no DOM, no node:fs, no page assumptions — that owns the cycle and exposes the seams the other placements need. lib/resolver.mjs becomes the first provider plugged into it rather than the thing that owns the flow. The extension integration point lives in this library (N10/N16/N17), because 'we will be able to build extensions just by using voice' means the voice path and the extension path are the same path.

VERIFY BY DRIVING: the same module instance driven from the browser page AND from node against the running server, producing the same decisions for the same inputs; plus a test that fails if the page's copy of the cycle drifts from the library's.

RELATED: N15 (harness delegates to harnesses), N10/N16/N17 (extensions), and the placement question (where tools RUN — docs/06 §3, still open).

title: Docs that reflect the system, and a MECHANISM that keeps them current (README + design + architecture)
description:
Paul, 2026-09-19 (voice note): 'I want to make sure that there's a very clear design document about how this is supposed to run and an architecture document that describes the architecture and is always up to date as well. And the design doc and readme need to be always up to date as well, with the current actual reflection of the system.'

WHY THIS IS URGENT RATHER THAN TIDY, demonstrated tonight: the README contradicted itself in two adjacent sections — 'What works today: ... streamed as PCM16 over /live to models/gemini-3.8-live ... with thinking' AND 'What does not work yet: No live model. The resolver is scripted; nothing calls Gemini Live.' BOTH TRUE, about different halves: the AUDIO path is live, the TURN path (POST /api/turn -> lib/resolver.mjs provider 'script') is a four-verb placeholder. The biggest gap in the product was invisible because the doc described the two halves as one thing. A reader of either line alone would see no gap.

DELIVERABLES:
1. docs/08-how-it-runs.md (or an equivalent name) — the DESIGN doc: how this is supposed to run. The operating model: what components exist, what starts what, ports and why, the dev environment, the single-host rule, and the invariants. Written from the code as it is tonight.
2. docs/07-architecture.md — the ARCHITECTURE doc: components (page, zero-dep server, resolver seam, live session, ws transport, audio worklet, workspace), the routes served, the data flow, the seams (registerResolver, the provider list), and where each file's authority lies.
3. README corrected: the audio path and the turn path stated SEPARATELY so one cannot read as 'done' while the other is a placeholder; 'what does not work yet' made accurate.
4. AND THE PART THAT MAKES IT STICK: a MECHANISM, not a discipline. Doc freshness must fail loudly somewhere. Precedent in isocan: scripts/roadmap.mjs regenerates docs/ROADMAP.md and the merge check asserts an EMPTY DIFF. Apply the same idea here: a check that fails when an enumerable claim in the docs drifts from the code — the resolver providers actually registered, the routes the server actually serves, the model id in lib/live-session.mjs, the files the page actually loads — plus generated blocks for anything enumerable rather than hand-maintained lists. A doc that is only kept current by remembering is a doc that will contradict itself again within a week.

RULES: the check must FAIL LOUDLY when it drifts (test it by perturbing a claim and watching it go red), and it must not be a tautology. Docs must describe the system as it IS, including the parts that are placeholders — 'the resolve seam is registered with provider script, which handles create/read/list' is a truthful sentence, and it is the sentence whose absence hid the gap.

title: The oplog cannot answer 'did my edit land?' — no record of an attempted-and-lost op
description:
Found by ds-flash-2 investigating Paul's failed item.addVersion (2026-09-19). Full finding: cap-evidence/isocan-iiq-investigation-20260919/FINDING.md.

WHAT HAPPENED: Paul was moving text between boxes when the write was refused as 'item.addVersion — internal error'. The text is NOT recoverable: the refusal was HomeUnreachableError (packages/server/src/home-link.ts:205), which refuses BEFORE applying, so nothing was half-written; and reading all eight canvases he touched today shows item.addVersion appears in NONE of them, including the 224-op work canvas. The ledger agrees with the mechanism.

THE GAP, in the investigator's words: 'a ledger that cannot answer "did my edit land?" is a gap in the thing this project is built on.' The oplog records what LANDED and has **no record of an op that was attempted and lost**. Three distinct classes exist in the code and the user sees none of them:
- HomeUnreachableError (:205) — 'the write was NOT made' → refused before applying
- HomeRefusedError (:225) → no partial local apply
- noteFailure (:1495) — a link could not be carried: ops WERE written and are NOT arriving
Only the first was his; the three are indistinguishable from outside, and the daemon's reasoned message is **rate-limited to one line per canvas per daemon process** (health.complained) and never reaches the CLI, which prints 'internal error'.

THE INSTRUMENT THAT WOULD CLOSE IT (a design decision, not a fix): a per-op delivery state — attempted / carried / refused — recorded so the question is answerable after the fact. Decide: is that an oplog field, a separate delivery ledger, or a UI surface that reads the link state? And does the CLI stop saying 'internal error' and start saying which of the three classes it was?

RELATED: isocan-iiq (the reporting defect), isocan-vab (the machine-wide cause — a self-dialing daemon exhausting the socket table, fixed and in review). Paul's own words when he reported it: 'One change did not go through: item.addVersion — internal error. The canvas now shows what the home has.'

comments.text: CLOSED — feat/attempted-lost @73460f0 (pushed; whole gate 202 tests: 201 pass + 1 environment skip, 0 fail; pre-push gate + page acceptance ALL CLEAR; porcelain empty). The delivery vocabulary is in the audit: every act past pre-flight is recorded BEFORE it applies (decision attempt, result pending, boot = the process generation); every outcome carries attempt back to it (allow with observed facts = CARRIED; refuse with rule id = REFUSED); a process death between attempt and outcome leaves a DANGLING attempt, and the next boot's sweep completes it AS LOST — by name, idempotently, because 'whether it landed' is then unknown and must not silently read as either success or refusal. The bead's three classes map: refused-before-apply and refused-with-no-partial are refused entries; attempted-and-vanished is lost. Driven: write -> attempt + carried outcome linked; dangling attempt from a dead generation -> lost completion named attempted-and-lost, idempotent; pre-flight refusal -> refusal entry, NO attempt (the act never entered the applying phase). LIMITS: the crash case is driven by its exact state (a pending entry from a dead generation), not by a timed SIGKILL; /api/call and the write verb carry attempt-first — other verbs (read/list) stay outcome-only, which is the right weight for read-only acts; the isocan CLI half of the bead (naming the three classes to the person) is isocan's side of the seam.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text: CONTINUITY ADDENDUM @73b1e4a (pushed; coord elevated finding 2 of the review): resumeLog no longer swallows-and-resequences. ENOENT = genuinely fresh (silent); ANY other read failure = a NAMED throw (audit-unreadable) — because a log that exists but cannot be read has an UNKNOWN continuation, and appending with a reset sequence would hand fresh numbers to entries with ancestors. logAct surfaces it: the entry is NOT written, the response carries logged:null + logRefused/logWhy, and the console names the break. Driven: chmod 000 on the audit file -> logged:null + audit-unreadable; mode restored -> the sequence continues FROM the log's last seq; no duplicate seqs in one instance's log. (The strictness found a real bug in the drive itself first: my own arithmetic assumed one entry per write — attempt-first writes log two.)

title: resolveInsideRoot is wrong AND unreachable: the doc names it as the containment boundary, nothing calls it, nothing tests it
description:
Found while answering PR #9's Copilot review comments, verified on main (a15557e6).

THE DEFECT — core/paths.ts:23-33:
  line 24: rejects only candidate === '.' or candidate === '..' (EXACT matches)
  line 27: resolved = root + '/' + candidate   <- string concatenation, not path resolution
  line 29: prefix check: resolved.startsWith(root + '/')
For candidate = '../../evil.sh': resolved = 'root/../../evil.sh', which DOES start with 'root/', so the check PASSES and the function returns ok:true for a path that escapes the root. The '..' segments are never collapsed, so the prefix check cannot see them.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A NORMAL BUG: line 28's own comment says 'The prefix check is the OPFS containment boundary'. docs/02-environment.md relies on it as the containment-preserving write path, and N20 says the picked-root path REUSES it. So a guard is documented as doing a job it cannot do — the shape where the weaker version of a guard is more dangerous than its absence, because its absence is visible.

CURRENT BLAST RADIUS — measured, not assumed: grep across *.ts/*.mjs/*.js finds NO callers. resolveInsideRoot is defined and never invoked, and there are no tests for it (a test would have shown up as a caller). So it is NOT exploitable today. The exposure is: the moment the picked-root write path actually uses it, the escape works, and the doc already tells the next reader that containment is handled here.

FIX: resolve the candidate properly and reject on the RESOLVED path (normalise '..' before the prefix comparison), or reject any candidate containing a '..' segment. Then a test with the counterfactual: '../../evil.sh' must be REFUSED — a test that cannot fail proves nothing, so the assertion must name the escaping string.

RELATED: PR #8 was merged to main at a15557e6, which is the same N20 content PR #9 rebuilds. So the fix belongs on a branch off a15557e6, and PR #9's disposition needs deciding by diff.
close_reason: Fixed and verified 2026-09-19: core/paths.ts now refuses any '..' segment at any depth rather than prefix-checking a concatenated string; landed on main (0d7b832, PR #10 merged at 4ef7bc1). Counterfactual both ways — old resolver 3 cases RED including the escaping assertion, fixed 6/6 with a positive control and an invariant test. k3 reviewed it independently and PASSED (reviewed ref 9fac1a8). The three claims were corrected too: the false comment on core/paths.ts:28, docs/02-environment.md, and the build-spec check now pointing at the test rather than a promise.
